Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 504 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2025) 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit 504 (WMU) covers an 
area of 2,704 km² and is located in north-central 
Alberta, in the Boreal Central Mixedwood and 
Dry Mixedwood natural subregions. 
The landcover in the area is dominated by broadleaf 
forests (47%). Agriculture (17%) is the predominate 
land use and is concentrated in the southern part of 
the unit. Approximately 530 km² of land within WMU 
504 has a provincial land use designation as ‘Key 
Wildlife Biodiversity Zone’, including portions of the 
White Earth Valley and Amisk River area. Given their 
localized size and distribution, these zones play a 
disproportionately large role in maintaining overall 
productivity of regional ungulate populations and are a 
source of biodiversity. These zones ensure that 
significant proportions of the breeding population 
survive to the next year (Environment and Sustainable 
Resource Development 2015). 
The objective of the 2025 aerial ungulate survey was 
to assess the status of ungulate populations (moose, 
white-tailed deer, and mule deer if adequate 
observations were obtained) in WMU 504 by estimating 
abundance, density, and the age-sex composition. 
Survey Method 
An aerial survey for ungulates was conducted 
February 4th–5th, 2025 using distance sampling 
techniques (Alberta Environment and Parks 
2016, Buckland et al. 2001, Thomas et al. 2010). 
A total of 57 north-south transect lines spaced 
1.2 km apart were flown with one Astar 
helicopter (Airbus AS350 SD2) for a total survey 
effort of 519 km. Ungulates were classified as 
male or female and by age class (adult or 
juvenile) when possible. Female moose were 
identified primarily the presence of a vulva patch. 
White-tailed deer were classified as male if 
antlers were present, and female if antlers were 
absent and accompanied by a juvenile. It is 
assumed that most males have cast antlers when 
late winter aerial surveys occur (Alberta 
Sustainable Resource Development 2010). The 
categories of ungulate activity (bedded, standing, 
moving), and canopy cover (0–33%, 34–66%, 
and >66%) within 10 m of the ungulate, were 
included as covariates to improve estimates 
associated with the survey. Other wildlife 
sightings were recorded, including 20 mule deer 
and 21 elk. 
Results 
Moo
se 
A total of 217 moose were observed in 143 groups 
and classified as 57 bulls, 108 cows, 48 calves, and 4 
unclassified. The estimated bull:cow:calf ratio was 
53:100:45. The estimated density was 0.624 
moose/km² (90% Confidence Interval (CI) 0.509–
0.765; Coefficient of Variation (CV) = 12.3%) and the 
estimated abundance was 1,688 moose (90% CI 
1,377–2,068; CV = 12.3%). Results are summarized 
in Table 1. 
White-tailed deer 
A total of 256 white-tailed deer were observed in 86 
groups and classified as 15 bucks (all with antlers), 33 
does, 22 fawns, and 186 unclassified. The estimated 
buck:doe:fawn ratio was 45:100:66, however, antler 
cast was assumed to be significant and the buck ratio 
is likely underestimated, while the fawn and doe ratio is 
underreported as deer tended to be in large groups 
during the survey that made individual classifications 
difficult. The estimated density was 0.983 white-tailed 
deer/km² (90% CI 0.723–1.337; CV = 18.7%) and 
estimated abundance was 2,658 white-tailed deer 
(90% CI 1,954–3,617; CV = 18.7%).
